zurna 為雙簧氣鳴樂器，以短圓柱簧片接於錐形銅管發聲，需高氣壓，並可用循環呼: The zurna is a double-reed aerophone: a short cylindrical reed is fitted to a conical brass tube. It needs high breath pressure, and circular breathing keeps the sound continuous. A beginner can work with the seven front holes and one thumb hole; the range is more than an octave and the instrument can be transposed. The lips can rest against a small disc, like the mouthpiece of a feeding bottle, to hold back the high-pressure air. Because the volume is continuous and the top notes are piercing, it is best practised with a bass drum, and it is mostly used outdoors.

土耳其嗩吶常見於土耳其、亞美尼亞、庫爾德等民間音樂與舞蹈，通常由達烏爾大鼓伴奏，: The Turkish zurna is common in the folk music and dances of Turkey, Armenia, the Kurds and others, usually accompanied by the davul bass drum, and it also appears outdoors at weddings and public celebrations. It played an important part in Ottoman mehter music and grew into the music of the Janissary band and of military music. It is used in the folk music of the Assyrians, Anatolia, Azerbaijan and elsewhere, and was once used to summon crowds for official announcements.
土耳其嗩吶為雙簧氣鳴樂器，短圓柱簧片綁於圓錐銅管，需高氣壓才能發聲，故音量幾乎持: The Turkish zurna is a double-reed aerophone: a short cylindrical reed is tied to a conical brass tube, and it takes high pressure to sound, so the volume is almost continuously high, piercing and carrying, and circular breathing keeps it going without a break. The bore is cylindrical and the bell follows a parabola, which focuses the sound forward, well suited to the open air. Seven front holes and one thumb hole give a range of more than an octave, and the instrument can be transposed. It belongs to the same family as the oboe, but is louder and more directional, and it is usually paired with a bass drum, which supplies the low frequencies and the rhythm.

The sounding body is a short cylindrical reed, tied at one end to the conical brass tube and flattened at the other into a narrow slit, where the sound is made. The sources do not state the materials of the bell, the fingerholes and the other parts.

It is recorded in Persia in the sixth century AD, and later spread to many countries with the expansion of Islam, playing an important part in Ottoman mehter music. In the sixteenth century the Central Asian shawm reached China under the name "sona"; it is also used in Kyrgyzstan, Syria and elsewhere. After the expansion of the Ottoman Empire the instrument reached the Balkans, Hungary and Western Europe, where the name and the construction changed while a similar form was kept. It is often paired with a bass drum and provides the melody for folk dances, and it has become an important instrument of Turkish, Armenian and Kurdish dance.

The Turkish zurna is an aerophone, H-S number 422.112, a double-reed woodwind. Its reed is short and cylindrical, tied to one end of a conical brass tube, with the other end flattened into a narrow slit; the body is cylindrical, the bell follows a parabola, and there are seven holes at the front and one for the thumb. Playing calls for high pressure, circular breathing is possible, the volume is high and piercing, and it is often played with a bass drum (davul). It is found in the folk music and dances of Turkey, Armenia, Azerbaijan, the Assyrians, the Kurds and others, and is also used at weddings, public celebrations, official announcements and military music.
